text: Before the story begins, let everyone hold a few akshatas in their palm — at the end they go on your head.
Long ago the devas and sages went to Lord Shiva and prayed for a chief who would keep obstacles away from every good endeavour.
Both Kumaraswamy and Vinayaka came forward for that honour.
Shiva said, "Whoever bathes in all the sacred rivers of the three worlds and returns first shall have it."
Kumaraswamy sped off at once on his peacock.
Vinayaka simply walked three circles around his parents and said, "My parents are all the sacred rivers, all the worlds."
Delighted with that devotion and that wisdom, Shiva made Vinayaka lord of the ganas.
It happened on Bhadrapada Shukla Chavithi — which is why every auspicious beginning starts with him.
That Chavithi day, Ganapati feasted contentedly on the undrallu and kudumulu brought by devotees of all three worlds, and set off at night for Kailasa on his little mouse.
A snake crossed the path; the mouse startled; the Lord tumbled, and his full belly burst open, scattering the sweets.
Unruffled, Ganapati gathered them all back, tied the very snake around his waist, and rose.
Watching all this from the sky, the Moon burst out laughing.
Angered, Ganapati declared, "Whoever looks upon you shall suffer false blame."
From that day the world stopped looking at the moon altogether, and life without moonlight grew miserable.
When the devas pleaded, the Lord relented: "Only on Bhadrapada Shukla Chavithi each year must the moon not be seen.
And even if someone sees it by mistake, let them do my vratam, hear the story of the Syamantaka jewel, and place akshatas on their head — no blame will touch them."
How true that was, even Sri Krishna himself learned in the Dvapara age.
On a Chavithi night, drinking milk, he saw the moon's reflection in his cup.
In those days King Satrajit had received the Syamantaka jewel by the Sun-god's grace — a divine gem that yielded gold every day.
Krishna suggested such a jewel belonged with the king, for the good of all — Satrajit refused.
Soon after, his brother Prasena wore the jewel out hunting.
A lion killed him and carried off the gem; Jambavanta, the great bear-king, slew the lion and took the jewel to his cave, tying it over his daughter's cradle as a plaything.
When Prasena never returned, the whisper spread: "Krishna must have killed him for the jewel."
That was the fruit of the Chavithi moon.
To clear his name Krishna went into the forest and traced the trail — Prasena's body, the lion's pawprints, and a cave beyond.
Inside, Krishna and Jambavanta fought for twenty-eight days.
At last, his strength failing, Jambavanta realised, "Only my Rama could overcome me so," and with tears offered the jewel — and his daughter Jambavati's hand.
Back in Dwaraka, Krishna told the full assembly everything and returned the jewel to Satrajit.
Ashamed, Satrajit gave his daughter Satyabhama in marriage to the Lord and offered the jewel too.
The false blame was washed away completely.
Then the sages asked, "If seeing the Chavithi moon brought such trouble even to you, what of ordinary people?"

Krishna replied, "Whoever worships Vinayaka on Bhadrapada Shukla Chavithi, hears this Syamantaka story, and places akshatas on their head — even if they glimpse the moon by mistake, no false blame will come near them that year."
The story is complete.
Now place the akshatas in your palm on your head — and let the elders place them on the children's heads.
